title: The Battle of Mount Gilboa and Saul's Death

date.label: Undated 1 Samuel narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: The Philistines fought against Israel; the men of Israel fled and fell down slain on Mount Gilboa.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Mount Gilboa is a ridge at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley (Jebel Fuquʿa / Har Gilboa), summits somewhat over 1,600 ft (~500 m); the town of Jezreel stands on a spur at its north-west end; Shunem, Endor, and Moreh lie to the north, Beth Shan to the east guarding the Jordan crossings.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Gilboa," read in full; "Valley of Jezreel," read in full.

claims.claim: The Jezreel valley is the only natural east–west passage through the central hill country, linking the coastal road with the Jordan, Gilead, and Damascus; it is fertile, open, chariot country.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Valley of Jezreel," read in full.

claims.claim: The Philistines slew Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons. Abinadab is Ishui in 1 Sam 14:49.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre; JFB on 1 Sam 31 (name variant).

claims.claim: The archers hit Saul and he was sore wounded of the archers (JPS: "in great anguish by reason of the archers"). The Philistine army combined infantry, archers, and chariots, and the archers decided the king's fate before close combat.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full; BiblicalTraining, "Philistines," read in part (government section); JFB on 1 Sam 31.

claims.claim: Saul, fearing abuse at the hands of "these uncircumcised," asked his armour-bearer to thrust him through; the armour-bearer refused, "for he was sore afraid"; Saul fell on his own sword, and the armour-bearer fell likewise on his sword and died with him.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: The tradition that the armour-bearer was Doeg is reported by JFB as "according to Jewish writers"; the text names no one, and the identification is unproven.
claims.evidence: JFB on 1 Sam 31.

claims.claim: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armour-bearer, and all his men, that same day together" — the book's own summary sentence for the day.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: The men of Israel on the other side of the valley and on the other side of the Jordan forsook the cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them. The defeat emptied the country, not only the battlefield.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre; JFB on 1 Sam 31 (the valley of Jezreel).

claims.claim: On the morrow the Philistines cut off Saul's head, stripped his armour, sent tidings "to publish it in the house of their idols, and among the people," put his armour in the house of the Ashtoreths, and fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: The Chronicler adds that Saul's head was put in the temple of Dagon; the Bible does not state where that temple was.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Gilboa," "Beth Shan," and "Philistines," read in full / in part.

claims.claim: Rowe's identification of two early Iron Age temples at Beth Shan as the Ashtoreths temple and the Dagon temple is accepted by some and disputed by others; the deities of the buildings cannot be identified with certainty.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Beth Shan," read in full.

claims.claim: The valiant men of Jabesh-gilead marched all night, took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth Shan, brought them to Jabesh, burned them there, buried the bones under the tamarisk-tree, and fasted seven days.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: Burning the bodies was not normal Israelite practice; the interpretations on record are prevention of further desecration, dealing with mutilated and exposed bodies, or the burning of spices as at later royal funerals — but the plain reading is that the bodies themselves were burned, and the text states no motive.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Jabesh Gilead," read in full; JFB on 1 Sam 31.

claims.claim: Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite at the start of his reign; the recovery of the bodies is presented as the repayment of that debt.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Jabesh Gilead," read in full.

claims.claim: The site of Jabesh-gilead is not settled; the name survives in Wadi Yabis, and Tell Abu Kharaz with Tell el-Meqbereh is the most widely favoured candidate; no inscription names the town.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Jabesh Gilead," read in full.

claims.claim: Beth Shan (Tell el-Ḥuṣn) was an Egyptian garrison town in the Late Bronze Age, allotted to Manasseh, its Canaanites not driven out; the narrative implies it was in Philistine hands or allied with them, but little distinctively Philistine material has been excavated there.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Beth Shan," read in full.

claims.claim: Samuel's verdict at Endor — "to-morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me" (28:19) — and David's prediction — "he shall go down into battle, and be swept away" (26:10) — are fulfilled in chapter 31; the chapter quotes neither. Both verses were verified in the Masoretic text in this session.
claims.evidence: Hebrew + JPS 1917 read in full (28:19; 26:10) and ch. 31, Mechon Mamre.

claims.claim: The Amalekite's account of Saul's death differs from 1 Sam 31:3–5 and is generally understood as invented for reward; David has the man executed for claiming to slay the LORD's anointed (2 Sam 1:14–16).
claims.evidence: 2 Sam 1:1–27 read in full, Mechon Mamre; BiblicalTraining, "Gilboa," read in full.

claims.claim: David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, the "lament of the bow," curses the mountains of Gilboa — "let there be no dew nor rain upon you" (1:21) — as poetry, not geography; its refrain is "How are the mighty fallen!"
claims.evidence: 2 Sam 1:1–27 read in full, Mechon Mamre; BiblicalTraining, "Gilboa," read in full.

claims.claim: David later moved the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh — from the public square at Beth Shan — and buried them in Kish's tomb at Zela. 2 Samuel 21 was not re-read in this dossier; the fact is recorded as the Beth Shan and Jabesh articles give it.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Beth Shan" and "Jabesh Gilead," read in full.

claims.claim: The Chronicler explains Saul's death as the consequence of unfaithfulness and of seeking counsel of a medium. The explanation is the Chronicler's, not 1 Samuel's; 1 Chr 10 was not re-read in full in this dossier.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Gilboa," read in full.

connections.note: The Philistines gather at Shunem and Saul camps on Gilboa; Saul is afraid, and the LORD answers him neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. The positions and the silence are set here.
Samuel's verdict at Endor: "to-morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me." The battle of Gilboa fulfils it, though the chapter never quotes it.
David is dismissed at Aphek while the battle is prepared. The dismissal is what puts David back at Ziklag while Saul fights at Gilboa; David is absent from chapter 31 entirely.
David recovers Ziklag while Saul fights at Gilboa. The two chapters run in parallel time, and the book tells them one after the other, not together.
David's prediction: Saul will go down into battle and be swept away. The chapter fulfils it without quoting it.
Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite, mustering Israel at Bezek and attacking in the last watch of the night. The men of Jabesh repay that debt when they recover his body.
Saul's sons are listed: Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. The Abinadab of 31:2 is the Ishvi of this verse, under a different name.
The Chronicler's parallel account of the battle and the death, adding the head in the temple of Dagon and the explanation that Saul died for his unfaithfulness.
David hears the news in Ziklag, mourns, executes the Amalekite who claims to have slain Saul, and laments Saul and Jonathan in the lament of the bow.
David blesses the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul and promises them kindness, noting that Judah has anointed him king. The blessing closes the Jabesh story.
David takes the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh and buries them in the tomb of Kish at Zela, with the executed descendants of Saul. The burial of chapter 31 is not the last resting place.
Targets Judges 4 and 5. Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera in the same Jezreel country, by the waters of Megiddo. The valley that saw Israel's victory under the judges now sees its king fall.
Gideon camps by the spring of Harod at the foot of Gilboa, with the Midianites to the north. The same ridge and the same spring frame both battles.

The Philistines defeat Israel at Ebenezer, capture the ark, and kill Eli's sons. The defeat at Gilboa is the second great Philistine victory of the book, and the first king dies as the first high priest's sons died.
